title: Rust's introduction, collecting ODJB records and checking label files
summary: Rust describes finding an ODJB record in 1936, collecting, the 1957 reissue, and his research in Victor and Columbia files showing the ODJB made the first jazz records; also dismisses Buddy Bolden recordings.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Today is Sunday, June 14th, 1959. This is Brian Rust of London, England. I'm sitting in the living room of Nick LaRocca's home, 2218 Constance Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. Mr LaRocca has done me the honour of making a tape recording of his voice telling his story of how he came to create jazz and his opinions and the whole story of the growth of the music. And he's asked me to give my side of it, how I came to be interested in the music and what it means to me and to English people now. Until 1936, I'd never heard of the original Dixieland jazz band. That year, on March 31st to be exact, I happened to discover in a London second-hand shop a copy, in very bad condition indeed, of At the Jazz Band Ball and Ostrich Walk on his master's voice record. It was one which had been made in New York in 1918. I'd never heard of the band and I took the record home. It cost exactly one penny. And I took the record home and played it and immediately I realised that I'd got something quite different from the ordinary dance music and popular music of the day, which interested me as far as it went. But this was something quite different. This was a new thing entirely, although it was then 18 years old. I made some enquiries and discovered that this was not the only record that the original Dixieland jazz band had made. But I was very upset to find that there wasn't one single record then in the catalogue that I could buy in brand new condition and so enjoy to the full. About six months later, without my asking for it, his master's voice reissued the famous original Tiger Rag. And I promptly bought that and they backed it up with Jasmine Blues, which again was the first recording of that number. And then a few months later still they issued some more. And although I didn't know it at the time, Mr. La Rocca had regrouped the original band and was in fact in 1936 itself recording some of the old numbers again under the modern electric system. And they were issued in England too. At least four of them were. Tiger Rag, Skeleton Jangle, original Dixieland One Step and Barnyard Blues. And of course, as soon as I realised they were on sale, I snapped them up. Well, of course, from there on, I started looking round for the real rarities. But being a schoolboy, I didn't have very much money to spare and I had to wait until I started work in 1940. And I started advertising for records and getting to know other collectors. And in fact, I started my expanding my circle of friends by answering an advertisement in the London Gramophone publication of June 1940. Because there was an advertisement in that which said, wanted records by the original Dixieland Jazz Band will buy them. And they followed an address which I wrote to. And we started comparing notes and one thing led to another. And I met another fellow who collected the records and who had nearly all of them. And including the 12-inch Columbias, which the band made in London in 1919 and 1920. And a bit later on, I discovered some of these for myself. And within about five years, I managed to get all of them, except the Aerelean Vocalians, which I still don't have. And one or two of the OKs, which I've managed to get since. Although, of course, the OKs were not made by the original band. They had Artie Seberg on clarinet and Henry Vanicelli on piano. A little while later, I presented a program on the air, two copies of which I've given to Mr. La Rocka, dealing with the influence of the original Dixieland Jazz Band on other bands. Some of them I put in for the sheer fun of the thing, because the bands were obviously striving to capture the spirit and the letter of the original jazz music without getting very far with it. Others made quite a good job of it. I featured records in this program of Muggsy Spanier and Sam Lannin and Bix Beiderbecq. And, generally speaking, the program was quite successful. Although, of course, having met Mr. La Rocka since, I've learned a great deal more about the truth of the origins of jazz than I knew at the time of making the broadcast. That was in 1954. In 1957, Columbia Graphophone Company in London asked me to lend them the original 12-inch recordings, because they wanted to transfer them to long-playing records and issue them on the market again, because they thought there would be a demand for them. And they were right. There was. All my copies were in perfect condition, and they made a very good transfer process. I sent a copy of the finished record to Mr. La Rocka, and he was very pleased with it. I wrote the sleeve note too, the liner note for it. And I'm afraid that a number of the facts that I put in there weren't facts at all. They were just the things that other people who knew less about the subject than I did had told me. And I received a letter from Mr. La Rocka in November 1957, putting me really wise on this subject. I really got the full details. And ever since then, I've had a stream of correspondence from him with the most wonderful enclosures, most of which are in the archives of the Tulane University. They were press cuttings, letters from musicians and important people, theatre bills, record supplements, and even pieces of music which had never been published. And this, of course, I very much appreciate. They occupy a very treasured place in my own library. Although I came to New Orleans in 1951, for one reason or another, I didn't get around to seeing Mr. La Rocka. There were certain people here who should be nameless, who deflected me from seeing him because they said that he wouldn't be of any interest in me. I ought to go and hear the real thing which amounted to a collection of very third-rate, or even ninth-rate musicians and old-timers who were leftovers from the ragtime and marching band era, which may have been all right in its time, but they can't play jazz. They just don't play jazz, let's face it. There's a very prevalent rumour going around that, in fact, it's a famous story perpetrated by numbers of writers and so-called historians in jazz, that the original Creole jazz, if that's the word, orchestra, under the direction of Freddie Kepard, recorded for Victor before the original Dixieland jazz band did. That is not so. When I was in New York last week, I was privileged to inspect the files of RCA Victor, the company which, so legend has it, made these records. They certainly made the original Dixieland jazz band records in February 1917, and I've checked on that and found that is so. In fact, everything that Mr. Larrakus told me ties in with the Victor files. I've gone into this thing very thoroughly, so I know exactly that everything he says is true. And when I was going through the volume of 1918 recordings, that is, the year after the first original Dixieland jazz band records, I found an entry which is rather interesting. Under the heading of Monday, December the 2nd, 1918, that is, nearly two years after the first original Dixieland jazz band recordings, I found an entry under the heading of the original Creole jazz band. It didn't give any names. It simply gave the instruments. I forget exactly what they were, but there was cornet, trombone, clarinet, piano, mandolin, I think, and drums, and one title, Tackin' Them Down, I think it was called. And it was described as a test record made for trial purposes, and it was stamped, Master Destroyed, Rejected. I made further inquiries to see if the record was available, to see what it sounded like. It was told that it was considered unsuitable for issue, and had long ago been destroyed, and that what the file said was true. There was no further reference to the original Creole jazz band, or in fact any other jazz band, apart from the Louisiana Five, and that was some time later on still. The only jazz band making records for Victor, or Columbia, because I inspected Columbia's files also, at that time, in fact between any time up to 1922 or 23, was the original Dixieland jazz band. There were no others. There were a number of copyists. There was Earl Fuller's so-called jazz band. Well, of course, we all have heard records of those, and we know exactly how unlike the original Dixieland jazz band they were. There was Ted Lewis's jazz band on Columbia, which was no more a jazz band than the Boston Promenade Orchestra. And there were a number of other complete phonies, let's say. There were no other genuine jazz bands on record at that time. I've inspected not only the Victor and Columbia files, but also those of the Edison Company, and of those of the Jeanette Company, the Star Piano Company of Richmond. I've inspected the OK files of the General Phonograph Corporation of New York. All these have been made available to me through the courtesy of the parent companies concerned. And most of the other famous recording companies, like Capitol and Decca, weren't even in existence at that time, let alone making records of jazz. So I would like to put on record the fact that in 1917, and from then on until 1922 or 1923, there is no trace whatever of any band having made jazz recordings, except the original Dixieland jazz band. And they made quite a large number, though for my money not enough. It's a great pity that certain of them, which are listed in the files as rejected, were never issued. I don't know whether the masters are still available. I imagine they can't be. But there was a Satanic Blues, there was a Lassie's Candy, and there was a tune called In the Dusk, none of which were ever published. And there were various alternative takes of the numbers that were published, which we don't seem to have had. Nevertheless, I'm more than delighted to be able to meet Mr. La Rocca, and to see his wonderful collection of press cuttings and all the other things, pictures, many of which have never been, never appeared in public before. And I'm looking forward very much to reading the book which my good friend Harry Brunn has written on the subject, because this will put the record straight once and for all. He's been into this question, I believe, for the last 20 years, so it should be a wonderful job of work. I can quite understand the difficulties that he was up against when he tried to get the book published before, because most publishers, so he tells me, wouldn't look at it, because it refused steadfastly to mention people like Buddy Bolden, who was put in the Louisiana State Asylum, I believe, in 1905 or thereabouts. And in that connection, incidentally, I've done a little research as well. I've done some technical work on his so-called recordings. He's supposed to have made some records, I believe cylinders or discs, some people say they were discs, before he was put in the loony bin in the crazy house. Well, he may have done. One thing is certainly he didn't make any flat discs, because I've been right the way through the Victor and Columbia files again. They were the only companies in existence at that time. And I've been through their files right the way back to 1900 when the firms began, and there is no sign of any records of Buddy Bolden. So much for the discs. It's absolutely unthinkable that any other company could have made discs at that time, because there just weren't any companies. They owned, the Victor and Columbia owned the patent rights to making disc records. Anybody else making them would have been stamped on at once. Nobody would have had that much financial backing in any case. So we know they can't have been discs that Mr Bolden had made. He may have made some private cylinders, but there again, if he did, it would be quite impossible, even if we found them nowadays, to play them. So that I think it's fair to say that his prowess, if any, must remain a beautiful legend, a fairy story designed for credulous people ready to believe that sort of thing. What we have got are recordings, which anyone can play, of the original Dixieland jazz band, and that's good enough. All right, so they weren't made in 1900, they were made in 1917. Never mind. They were good enough, and good enough for anybody to listen to. They're jazz, that's what matters, and they're the first jazz. And until then, there was no jazz. There was ragtime, yes. There were ragtime piano rolls, there were a few ragtime recordings. But there were a few recordings by coloured bands. There was Jim Europe on Victor, there was Wilbur Sweatman on Columbia, there was Ford Dabney on a number of different labels, mostly Aeolian and Vecalian. But one's only got to listen to those. They're not easy, they're not difficult to find.
